summary: Fox frames the problem: ambient scribes run in roughly a third of US practices with near-zero adverse event reporting, so errors sit silently. He categorizes failures into transcription mishearings and generator-side additions, changes, and omissions; the hard versions of all three share one problem—judging whether a difference actually matters. That clinical taste is tacit, contextual, and moving, so it cannot be pre-specified in a fixed rubric. A generator-plus-checker exploits the asymmetry of verification, but only for spotting differences; deciding which matter is harder than writing the note. His strongest judge—a frontier model with a detailed faithfulness rubric, automatic rubric optimization, and deterministic concept counting—still waved through roughly one in five notes containing serious errors, typically omissions, because it can be faithful to the words while lying about the intent. Identical omissions (a France holiday vs. a Lake Malawi trip in a hematuria workup) carry opposite clinical weight. Fox rejects the two obvious places to store taste: prompt-stuffing a perfect rubric (just shown to fail) and baking it into weights (goes stale, opaque, requires retraining whenever the standard moves). Instead he proposes keeping the standard as examples and assembling a case-specific one per output. The repeating loop has three steps: Discover failure modes by running the system in production and clustering real outputs (synthetic cases only cover imagined failures; the painful ones are unanticipated), Capture expert judgment on real outputs in focused sessions—comments, reasoning, corrections, not just scores—and Calibrate each new output by retrieving the most similar prior judgments, expert corrections, and relevant guidelines into the judge's context. He demonstrates this on the opening headache note: nearest cases of red flags filed as routine, the relevant correction that new headache over 50 demands red-flag review, and applicable guidelines make the dropped jaw claudication obvious—not because the model is smarter, but because it now knows what matters. Comparing three judges on the same dataset, the off-the-shelf rubric judge is barely better than chance, the 'serious' rubric-plus-deterministic-checks system improves but still misses much, and the loop-driven judge performs substantially better. The difference is not compute or prompting; it is fitting the standard to each case and keeping it alive. Fox closes by generalizing beyond clinical notes: any high-stakes AI output (contract review, support agents) faces the same problem and the same remedy. Evaluation is not a thing to build once and freeze but a continuous loop—stop trying to write the standard down in advance, capture it case by case, and evolve it.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The note that looks completely fine
sections.summary: Fox presents a real ambient-scribe note that reads as a routine tension headache but silently omits the patient's jaw pain on chewing—a giant cell arteritis red flag that can cause blindness within days and demands same-day steroids. Nothing in the note is wrong; the danger is what is missing. He then introduces himself: medical doctor, now at Composo building AI evaluation for high-stakes domains.

sections.title: The obvious errors, and how common they are
sections.summary: A not-so-subtle case follows: a 20-something tonsillitis note fabricates chest pain, suspected angina, fictional diabetes meds, and a non-existent hospital, leading weeks later to a real diabetic eye-screening invite. Fox cites the largest real-world study: ~1 in 20 notes carry harm-grade errors, ~1 in 5 have important omissions, and >1 in 10 contain hallucinations. Ambient scribes are in ~1/3 of US practices with near-zero adverse event reporting, so the field is 'flying blind.' The pattern generalizes beyond healthcare to any high-stakes AI use.

sections.title: Mapping every failure across three production scribes
sections.summary: Fox plots every failure found across three leading production ambient scribes on a chart of clinical severity vs. automated-check detectability. Most failures sit below the line—uncaught—and the dangerous quadrant is bottom-right: high-stakes and missed.

sections.title: Mishearings, additions, changes, omissions
sections.summary: He walks through examples: 'it just happened' recorded as 'abrupt sudden onset' (driving a hemorrhage workup); a plan to hold off tests in favor of antibiotics recorded as 'arrange tests today.' He distinguishes transcription-layer mishearings (Humalog/Humulin, hyper-/hypothyroidism, 'no evidence of cancer' → 'evidence of cancer') from generator-side additions, changes, and omissions. The blatant forms are easy to catch; the hard part across all three is judging whether the difference matters.

sections.title: The hard part is knowing what matters
sections.summary: Fox reframes clinical judgment as tacit, contextual, and moving: a missed allergy can kill in one note and be irrelevant in another; guidelines and even good doctors disagree. Models know the facts but lack a sense of what matters for this specific example.

sections.title: Put a checker after the generator
sections.summary: Because generation is cheap, Fox argues for a checker after the generator, exploiting the asymmetry of verification. The best teams build serious evaluators: frontier judges with detailed faithfulness rubrics (worked pass/fail examples), rubric auto-optimization, and deterministic NLP concept counting.

sections.title: The best judge waved a fifth of them through
sections.summary: Running that best-judge system over his earlier notes, it scored most fine and signed off the rest, yet ~1 in 5 'clean passes' still hid a serious error, usually an omission. The judge isn't blind or stupid—it faithfully reports the words (e.g., 'start amoxicillin' was discussed) while lying about intent. A naïve judge becomes a second silent failure nodding along with the first. The verifier is only cheaper for the easy half (spot differences); deciding which differences matter is harder than writing the plausible note.

sections.title: France versus Lake Malawi
sections.summary: Two patients with hematuria each had a dropped holiday line—France vs. Lake Malawi. France is noise; Lake Malawi (freshwater, sub-Saharan Africa) is schistosomiasis until proven otherwise and changes management. Identical omissions, opposite clinical weight—this context-bound judgment cannot be pre-specified in a rubric.

sections.title: Discover, capture, calibrate
sections.summary: If taste cannot be written down, it must be learned from examples, analogous to RLHF. Fox lists three places to store learned taste: prompt-stuff a perfect rubric (just shown to fail), bake it into weights via fine-tuning/continual learning (problematic while the standard keeps moving)—the section ends as he continues this comparison.

sections.title: Store taste as examples, not specifications or weights
sections.summary: Fox rejects the two obvious places to keep taste. A baked-in score is wrong: weights go stale, cannot explain themselves, and cannot be updated without a retrain. Prompt-stuffing a perfect rubric has just been shown to fail. The third option is to keep the taste as the examples themselves—past judgments, expert corrections, references—and for each output retrieve the ones that bear on it into the judge's context. Add one and it is live on the next call, with an exact pointer to what moved the score. It is both better and cheaper for this problem.

sections.title: Discover: cluster real production outputs into a failure-mode ontology
sections.summary: The loop's three steps are discover, capture, calibrate. Discovery is not whiteboard guessing: you must run the system in production, look at real outputs, and cluster what goes wrong. The failure modes surface on their own and you name them—this is your failure-mode ontology. Real-world failure modes are effectively unbounded, and synthetic test cases only cover the failures you already imagined; the ones that hurt are the ones you did not think to check for, and you only find them in real outputs. The ontology becomes your map of what to capture judgment on and what to retrieve against.

sections.title: Capture: focused expert sessions on real outputs
sections.summary: Capture is the simple part. Put real outputs in front of your experts; clinicians can spend a focused few hours leaving comments. It does not have to be a month-long labeling project to start with. Collect their judgment—not just a score but the reasoning and corrections—and over time build up the record of how your experts actually judge. The discovered failure modes are not a checklist the judge runs, but they organize everything: what to ask experts about and how to index the cases you will retrieve.

sections.title: Calibrate: assemble a case-specific standard for each output
sections.summary: Calibration is the generic part you can write down once—be faithful, do not drop anything important—but what counts as a serious miss for this specific note is contextual and shifts from note to note. So you assemble it on the fly: the judging agent pulls in everything that bears on this one case, its memory of the most similar outputs it has judged before and how they scored, the expert corrections that apply, and the reference documents and guidelines. It is context engineering per output—not one pre-specified rubric in a vacuum, not a model you have to retrain every week, but a case-specific standard assembled for the output. It is a loop: every output judged and every correction sharpens the next, and when a brand-new failure mode appears, discovery surfaces it and it flows straight back in.

sections.title: Re-running the opening headache note through the loop
sections.summary: To make this concrete, Fox returns to the opening headache note that hid a possible blindness emergency. The loop-driven judge pulls in the nearest cases experts have judged—not this exact patient but the same shape, a red flag filed as routine—the corrections that apply, such as a new headache over 50 needing a red-flag check, and the relevant criteria and guidelines. The model has not memorized the case; given the right context to reason from, the dropped red flag stands out. It was never actually hard to catch—it just did not know what mattered.

sections.title: Three judges on the same notes
sections.summary: Passing the original generated-note dataset through three judging systems, the off-the-shelf rubric frontier judge is better than a coin flip but misses most of what matters; the 'serious' rubric-plus-deterministic-checks system is better again but still misses a lot; and the loop-driven judge with discovered failure modes calibrated per output performs substantially better. The notes are the same; only what the judge was shown changes. The difference is not more compute or a better prompt—it is that the first two fight taste and lose (guessing criteria, freezing one standard, going stale) while the evolving loop discovers the modes, fits the standard to each, and keeps learning.

sections.title: Beyond healthcare: the same pattern in any high-stakes AI
sections.summary: Even if you do not write clinical notes, if you ship anything where being confidently wrong has a cost—contract review that misses the clauses that change the deal, support agents that promise refunds you do not offer—the same problem and the same remedy apply. Three takeaways: discover your failure modes from real outputs, do not guess them; capture your experts' judgment on them, the standard they cannot write down; calibrate every output against the cases they have already judged, not a static rubric and not a retrained model. The easiest place to start is having experts leave free-form comments on real outputs—that is the raw material for everything else. Your judge can verify anything you write down in advance, but the standard of good never could be, so stop trying to write it all down in advance and instead capture it case by case and evolve it. Evaluation is not something you have but something you do continuously over time.

limitations: Pre-specified rubrics can only encode taste that can be articulated, missing the tacit, contextual, moving judgment that drives clinical decisions.
Generator-plus-checker is only cheaper for the easy bit (spotting differences); deciding which differences matter is harder than generation.
Models can be 'faithful to the words but a lie about the intent,' passing naive verifiers while mis-representing clinical decisions.
Baked-in weights go stale, cannot explain their scores, and require a retrain to update as the standard moves.
Synthetic test cases only cover failures already imagined; the ones that hurt are the unanticipated ones found only in real outputs.
Adoption is outpacing safety: errors are common but almost none surface as reported incidents.
